data.description:

The Two Stellantis Stories Investors Were Choosing Between

The shares cost €9.41 at the start of the period, and anyone looking at Stellantis then had to decide which story about the future sounded more realistic.

On the upbeat side, the bull Narrative argued for a Fair Value of €14, assuming an 11.0% annual revenue growth rate and a shift from a loss of €2.4b to earnings of €12.5b by around 2028.

The bear Narrative put Fair Value at €6, based on a slower 3.5% yearly revenue growth rate and concern that reliance on internal combustion vehicles would keep pressure on margins.

What The Results Changed In The Stellantis Debate

Stellantis swung from a net loss of €4.5b in Q3 2025 to a smaller €535m loss in Q3 2026, with net margin improving from -12.2% to -1.4%. That supported the more optimistic view of a recovery in earnings power. However, profitability was still negative, which kept the cautious view on sustainable margins very much alive. Overall, the evidence pointed in both directions.

The key assumption was how quickly Stellantis could turn higher shipments and revenue into solid profits. For any automaker making big promises, it is important to check whether net margin actually moves decisively into positive territory and remains there before treating an earnings recovery story as established.

What Today’s Stellantis Price Already Assumes

Today Stellantis trades at €3.52, after a year to date loss of 63.7%. The current Narrative’s Fair Value sits above that level, which is the author’s assessment rather than a settled fact.

According to FRAGMENTS, an investor in the Simply Wall St Community, the key question now is whether the industrial operations can generate steady cash without burning more capital. A buyer today would need to believe industrial profitability and free cash flow can recover and stay positive in North America and Europe.

"The considerable discount to book value deserves attention, but further industrial cash consumption could materially reduce the value available to ordinary shareholders. The most important evidence will be sustained improvements in North American and European margins, lower warranty costs and positive Industrial free cash flow generated internally rather than through additional financing."

data.description:

iShares U.S. Pharmaceuticals ETF (IHE)

Holdings: 56 | In pharmaceuticals: 99.5% of the fund

This ETF leans hard into the GLP-1 theme through Eli Lilly, a large diabetes and obesity drug company at 26.59% of the portfolio. Johnson & Johnson adds another 22.16% with a broad mix of medicines and medical products that are not tied to one therapy. Viatris at 4.85% brings a focus on established treatments and generic drugs. Rising use of GLP-1s on government plans could affect the more concentrated Eli Lilly position most, while the other holdings link your exposure to a wider range of pharmaceuticals.

VanEck Pharmaceutical ETF (PPH)

This ETF focuses on the pharmaceuticals opportunity with a more mixed lineup than IHE. Eli Lilly at 23% and Novo Nordisk at 5.42% provide exposure to two large GLP-1 players tied directly to the heavier prescription use that is troubling the US Treasury. Merck at 12.15% adds a sizable position that is less dependent on weight loss drugs and more on a broader portfolio of medicines. About 47% of PPH overlaps with IHE, while the rest tilts into other pharmaceutical businesses, health care distributors, and a small allocation to biotech that IHE does not cover.

Investors are relying on a fund where pharmaceuticals account for 86.8% of the assets, and Eli Lilly and Merck together make up 35.1% of the weight. State Street Health Care Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLV)

About 37% of its money overlaps with PPH; however, the extra weight in health care equipment and services means the impact of higher GLP-1 spending is mixed with other health care trends.

You are relying on a basket where Eli Lilly and Johnson & Johnson together are 26.8% of the fund, so the GLP-1 story and wider drug spending shape a meaningful slice of XLV, but much of the ETF still depends on devices, tools and managed care businesses whose fortunes may not move in step with that theme.

If you want the GLP-1 story front and center, IHE gives you the most concentrated pharmaceuticals exposure at 99.5% of the fund and the heaviest single position in Eli Lilly. PPH sits close by with 86.8% in pharmaceuticals and more overlap with IHE at the top, while also mixing in distributors and a bit of biotech. XLV is different. Only 37.2% is in pharmaceuticals, with large slices in biotechnology, equipment, tools and managed health care that pull attention away from GLP-1 drugs.

One practical condition has to hold for this theme to matter: demand from patients on government programs needs to become sustained prescriptions, otherwise tighter coverage or pricing terms could blunt any benefit for drugmakers. All three ETFs ended the past five years within 4.8 percentage points of each other, and the annual fee gap from US$8 to US$37 on a US$10,000 holding is modest. data.title: Which ETFs Give You Alphabet After The Air Force Cloud Breach?
data.description:
You might like Alphabet for its search, video and cloud businesses, but owning the stock alone means carrying Alphabet specific risks by yourself. Simply Wall St flags that further fines, product limits or forced changes to how it runs search and ads could cut into advertising reach and money made from artificial intelligence. Holding Alphabet inside a fund that spreads your money across many holdings changes how much those single company risks can move your overall portfolio, and also limits how much upside Alphabet can drive on its own.

Right now the headline is security. Hackers breached the US Air Force Cloud One system that runs on infrastructure from Alphabet and other tech giants, disrupting upgrades and touching sensitive data. That kind of event affects how customers think about cloud reliability and how they choose providers. If you still want Alphabet in that mix, exchange-traded funds (ETFs) such as IWF, VUG and IVW give you a way to own it as part of a wider portfolio rather than on its own.

Picking stocks directly instead? Compare Alphabet with 52 AI infrastructure stocks.

iShares Russell 1000 Growth ETF (IWF)

IWF tilts heavily toward US growth sectors, with large slices in semiconductors, interactive media, hardware and software. Alphabet is a meaningful part of that mix at 9.96% of the portfolio, so each US$1,000 in IWF puts about US$100 into Alphabet. A large share of the remaining exposure runs through other sizeable tech and growth stocks such as NVIDIA and Apple, which together make up 21.1% of the fund and shape much of its tech-heavy profile.

Alphabet’s high level of non-cash earnings can make its reported profits harder to interpret, because items such as accruals and stock-based pay can blur the relationship between earnings and cash. IWF addresses that company-specific characteristic primarily by pairing Alphabet with businesses whose profits depend on different products and customers, for example NVIDIA’s chip demand and Apple’s hardware and services. The fund still concentrates meaningfully in large US growth franchises whose cash flows are used to support their current valuations.

Vanguard Morningstar Growth ETF (VUG)

Apple and NVIDIA dominate VUG’s roster, together covering 26.5% of the ETF and pulling a lot of your exposure toward semiconductors and hardware. The broader mix looks a lot like IWF, with large slices in semiconductors, technology hardware, systems software and interactive media. Alphabet sits behind those giants as the #4 position at 7.97% of the portfolio, so each US$1,000 in VUG quietly puts about US$80 into Alphabet while the rest spreads across 141 holdings.

Alphabet still faces the risk that extra fines, tighter rules or changes to how it runs search and ads could limit advertising reach and AI related income. VUG will not cancel that. However, its stakes in areas such as pharmaceuticals, automobile manufacturers and transaction and payment processing services mean more of your money relies on different industries than Alphabet alone offers.

iShares S&P 500 Growth ETF (IVW)

IVW gives Alphabet a real slice at 9.08% of the portfolio, so each US$1,000 puts about US$91 into the stock. The rest of the money tracks a growth-heavy mix that closely resembles VUG, with 21.8% in semiconductors, 13.1% in systems software and 8.2% in technology hardware, storage and peripherals. NVIDIA and Microsoft together take 22.8% of IVW, while pharmaceuticals, broadline retail and multi sector holdings add exposure to different drivers than Alphabet’s search and ads.

If customers slow AI adoption, cut cloud spending or hold back on TPU style systems, Alphabet’s cloud related revenue and group earnings could disappoint. IVW still carries that risk through its 9.08% stake in Alphabet, but its positions in sectors such as pharmaceuticals and retail tie more of the outcome to healthcare demand and consumer spending patterns instead of a single company’s AI and cloud story.

Choosing your Alphabet exposure through funds

If you want Alphabet in size without stock picking, IWF and IVW sit closest together. Each US$1,000 puts roughly US$100 or US$91 into Alphabet and both charge US$18 a year on a US$10,000 holding. The real split is what surrounds it. IWF leans harder into semiconductors and hardware, while IVW spreads more into pharmaceuticals and multi sector holdings.

VUG asks a different question. It holds fewer companies than IWF and IVW, charges about US$3 a year on US$10,000 and tilts more toward its biggest positions. That can matter if a cyber incident like the recent Air Force cloud breach changes how investors view large tech platforms. Your first decision is simple. Do you want the extra concentration, or would you rather pay more to spread Alphabet’s cloud and advertising risks, including its high level of non cash earnings, across more holdings?
